plan.contextChunk: This figure places two geometric constructions side by side, labeled (a) and (b), both concerning light leaving a pair of narrow slits. In (a) a vertical tan bar at the left represents the slit barrier, with its two openings marked S1 and S2 and their separation bracketed as d. A gray vertical bar at the right is labeled Screen, and the horizontal gap between barrier and screen is bracketed below as D. Two teal rays, r1 from S1 and r2 from S2, each carrying a short drawn wave train, converge on a black dot labeled P on the screen. A dashed horizontal line runs from the midpoint between the slits to the point C on the screen, the vertical offset from C up to P is bracketed as y, and a dashed line from the slit midpoint to P makes the angle theta with that horizontal. Panel (b) magnifies the region just beyond the barrier: the same two openings, again separated by d, send rays now drawn parallel, each labeled to P and each inclined at theta to its own dashed reference. A dashed segment runs from the upper slit onto the lower ray at a marked right angle, isolating the short extra stretch labeled delta l. Enlarging the near-slit geometry beside the full layout shows that only the small difference delta l, not the lengths of r1 and r2 themselves, decides how the waves combine at P.

interactionPlan.concept: At a screen point P the two slit waves combine according to their path difference Δl = d sin θ, where the observation angle θ is fixed by the screen height y (tan θ = y/D); only this small extra length, not the long path lengths r1 and r2, decides constructive versus destructive interference.

interactions.label: Screen point height y
interactions.teaches: Moving P up the screen increases the observation angle θ, which lengthens the extracted path difference Δl — linking where you look on the screen to how far out of step the two waves arrive

interactions.label: Slit separation d
interactions.teaches: Widening the gap between S1 and S2 scales Δl proportionally at the same angle, making the relation Δl = d sin θ visible as a direct proportionality

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Zooming to the near-slit region shows the two long unequal rays becoming effectively parallel, collapsing the geometry into a single small right triangle whose short leg is exactly the path difference Δl

demo_steps.title: The full layout
demo_steps.narration: Light from slits S1 and S2 travels unequal distances r1 and r2 to reach point P on the screen; the vertical offset y sets the angle θ. The question is what controls whether the waves add or cancel at P.

demo_steps.title: Drag the screen point
demo_steps.narration: Slide y upward: P climbs the screen, θ opens up, and the path difference grows. The interference condition at P is governed by θ, which is fixed by where on the screen you observe.

demo_steps.title: Widen the slits
demo_steps.narration: Now increase d at the same screen point: the rays splay more and Δl grows in proportion, illustrating Δl = d sin θ. Both y (through θ) and d scale the same decisive quantity.

demo_steps.title: Zoom to the slits
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the magnified view: because the screen is far away the two rays are essentially parallel, and a perpendicular from the upper slit isolates a tiny right triangle. Its short leg Δl is the entire path difference — the long lengths r1 and r2 cancel out of the interference condition.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Interference at P depends only on the tiny path difference Δl = d sin θ extracted from a small right triangle near the slits — not on the long individual path lengths — and θ is set by the screen height y while d scales the result.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels. Panel (a): thin tan vertical barrier at left with two gaps S1/S2 and a 'd' bracket; thick gray vertical 'Screen' bar at right; 'D' double-arrow along the bottom; two teal rays r1, r2 from the slits converging on a black dot P, each ray carrying a small sinusoidal wave-train squiggle; dashed horizontal midline to C with a 'y' bracket up to P and a dashed midpoint-to-P line marking angle θ. Panel (b): same two openings with a 'd' bracket, two parallel teal rays labeled 'to P' each at angle θ to a dashed horizontal reference, a dashed perpendicular from the upper slit meeting the lower ray at a marked right angle, and the short leftover segment labeled Δl. Use teal for rays, tan for the barrier, gray for the screen and dashed construction lines, black for P and labels; keep both panels live-linked to the same y, d, θ so the sliders update both views consistently.

- Slider for screen point P height y: learner drags P up and down on the screen; rays r1 and r2 pivot, theta changes, and the extracted path difference delta l lengthens or shrinks in the side construction; the link between observation angle and interference path difference becomes clear.
- Slider for slit separation d: learner widens or narrows the gap between S1 and S2; the ray geometry and delta l segment update for the same screen point; the proportional relationship delta l = d sin(theta) becomes visible.
- Toggle between full apparatus and near-slit approximation: learner switches between the screen-scale view and the parallel-ray magnification; the long unequal paths collapse into the small right-triangle segment delta l; the approximation shows why only the extra path length controls constructive or destructive interference.

authoredContext:
The figure(a) shows how to determine the path length difference Δl for waves traveling from two slits to a common point on a screen. If the screen is a large distance away compared with the distance between the slits, then the angle θ between the path and a line from the slits to the screen [part (b)] is nearly the same for each path. In other words, r1 and r2 are essentially parallel. The lengths of r1 and r2 differ by Δl, as indicated by the two dashed lines in the figure. Simple trigonometry shows

where λ is the wavelength of the light, d is the distance between slits, and θ is the angle from the original direction of the beam as discussed above. We call m the order of the interference. For example, m=4 is fourth-order interference.

(a) To reach P, the light waves from S1 and S2 must travel different distances. (b) The path difference between the two rays is Δl.

Left picture is a schematic drawing that shows waves r1 and r2 passing through the two slits S1 and S2. The waves meet in a common point P on a screen. Distance between points S1 and S2 is d; distance between the screen with the two slits and the screen with point P is D. Point P is higher than the mid-point between S1 and S2 by the distance y. Imaginary line drawn from the point P to the mid-point between slits form an angle Theta with the x axis. Right picture is a schematic drawing that two slits separated by the distance d. Waves pass through the slits and travel to the screen P. Angle theta is formed by the travelling wave and x axis.

The equations for double-slit interference imply that a series of bright and dark lines are formed. For vertical slits, the light spreads out horizontally on either side of the incident beam into a pattern called interference fringes (the figure).
